#2705. The Cowboys and the cruel art of collapse

The Dallas Cowboys are bad at football. That's a tough reality to live in. For months we have been clinging to the hope that a stellar offense with a gradually improving defense would be the magic ticket to help this team pick up steam and start rolling down the stretch of the season. We have some bad news. Nothing's rolling.

The defense remains terrible, and the offense has started to join in by underperforming at unpopular moments in the game. The whole thing culminates in disappointing outings and losses to what we think are inferior teams. One after the other.

The latest letdown elevates the frustration to another notch. That's because it appeared like they were onto something by building a 14-point lead, but things inevitably fell apart. What happened this time? Taking a closer look paints an uncomfortable picture.

To start off, it's important to note that these two teams aren't too far off when it comes to ability. They both now have the same record, and this one went down to the wire, so it tracks. That's why it was misleading when the Cowboys got off to an early lead. It wasn't because of sheer dominance. It was just luck.

When you look at what went on early in the game, the Cowboys benefited greatly when a Jonathan Mingo muffed punt bounced right back into his hands. They were also fortunate that backup tight end James Mitchell was right there to fall on a Javonte Williams fumble in the end zone. Even Shemar James' interception that he returned deep into Arizona territory bounced right into his arms after it deflected off the Cardinals' receiver. You could make a strong case that this game would've remained a lot tighter had the ball bounced a little differently.

But hey, that's football, and Cowboys fans certainly aren't going to complain when some breaks go their way. The Cardinals kept dropping passes, committed a lot of false starts at terrible times, and even shanked the game-winning extra point at the end of regulation. Bad teams do bad things, and the Cardinals did their fair share.

Offensively, you might be inclined to think the Cowboys scored 30 points and that's more than enough. The offense did their part. But did they? They did score six times, three touchdowns and three field goals, but a close look shows the offense didn't look all that great. One of their touchdowns came from that before mentioned fumble recovery in the end zone, and the only reason they were down that far was because of the interception return.

The Cowboys' other two touchdowns came from improv plays where Dak Prescott started to scramble. In fact, on one of those scrambles, he ran into the end zone. When you step back, you see an offense that sputtered quite a bit. They didn't have any creative play calls to free up players. They often didn't have the correct protection set up, giving Cardinals defenders free shots in the backfield. And even when they just needed to get one lousy first down to run out the clock, they couldn't pull it off.

The result was 261 total yards against the defense that gives up the most points in the league. An offense with Prescott, CeeDee Lamb, George Pickens, and several first-round offensive linemen couldn't get the job done in critical moments. As unimpressive as this unit was, they were still outfailed by the defense.

Oh, the defense. What a weird game it was for this group. It's weird because, unlike the offense, they were never meh. They were either great or dreadful. There was no in-between. They started off really sharp. The pressure was there, the coverage was decent, and they were making hard-hitting tackles. The Cardinals couldn't get anything going. To understand this, let's offer some perspective.

With 90 seconds left in the first half, the Cowboys led 14-0. The Cardinals hadn't scored any points yet. With 90 seconds left in the third quarter, the Cowboys led 17-3. The Cardinals only had a field goal through almost three quarters of football. The defense finished with five sacks and two takeaways. They were making plays, but then they went from playing really well to absolutely horrid. What happened?

This is the frustrating part. The Cowboys got comfortable. Instead of playing disciplined, sound football, they wanted to annihilate the Cardinals and got caught overpursuing. On the big running plays, it was a collection of failures. The defensive line didn't maintain their gaps. Instead, they were aggressive and attacked upfield. With holes available, the defensive backs took poor angles and completely whiffed with their tackling. Manageable gains turned into monster plays for the Cardinals.

Those two big running plays allowed Arizona to get back in the game because they were fast strikes. And when the Cowboys offense couldn't finish things on their end, the Cardinals were given more chances to attack, and the defense wasn't equipped to fend them off.

Many will say that Minshew Mania saved the day. That's not what went down. Sure, credit Minshew for making plays, but he wasn't pulling off any Houdini escapes or threading any needles. He just calmly capitalized on coverage breakdowns by the Cowboys' defense. On the Cardinals' final two touchdowns, one to Trey McBride and another to Michael Wilson, there wasn't a defender anywhere close on either play. It was easy, and quite honestly, we all watched helplessly knowing it was coming.

If there's a silver lining, it's that the Cowboys do have talented pieces. Unfortunately, that doesn't mean anything if this team can't find a way to use them correctly. Both the offense and defense are having mental lapses and breakdowns. And it keeps happening week after week with no end in sight.

#2696. Man United 3-2 Roma: Cunha Inspires Remarkable Champions League Comeback

Manchester United have spent much of this season searching for evidence that their revival under Michael Carrick possesses genuine substance. On a remarkable Champions League evening at Old Trafford, they found something to believe in.

A dramatic 3-2 victory over Roma ended Man United's nine-match winless run, with Matheus Cunha scoring twice late on to complete a comeback that had seemed improbable during a dreadful opening period.

For Carrick, the result offered both encouragement and considerable cause for concern. His side demonstrated resilience, attacking ambition and renewed confidence after the interval. Yet the defensive vulnerabilities that threatened to undermine their European campaign remain painfully obvious.

Roma required just 11 minutes to establish control. Kobbie Mainoo surrendered possession in midfield, allowing Matias Soule to exploit the space behind Diogo Dalot and finish confidently beyond Senne Lammens.

United's defensive organisation deteriorated further when Soule again found himself unmarked. His subsequent effort struck Ayden Heaven's arm, presenting Donyell Malen with the opportunity to double Roma's advantage from the penalty spot.

Never before had Man United conceded twice so quickly in a European fixture at Old Trafford.

Dalot's positioning was particularly troubling. His repeated ventures forward left Heaven covering considerable ground, while Harry Maguire struggled to organise a defensive unit increasingly vulnerable to Roma's movement.

Bruno Fernandes eventually provided some relief. Having initially seen his penalty saved, the Portuguese midfielder benefited from defensive encroachment and converted the retake.

Even so, the boos accompanying United's departure at half-time reflected the frustration surrounding another disjointed performance.

Carrick's players emerged with greater purpose after the interval, pressing Roma more aggressively and moving possession with considerably greater urgency.

Carlos Baleba threatened following an impressive individual run, although an apparent hamstring injury subsequently forced his withdrawal. Youri Tielemans entered and helped establish greater control through midfield.

Cunha became increasingly influential as United committed more players forward. His equaliser followed a disastrous Roma defensive mistake, rewarding the Brazilian's anticipation and willingness to occupy dangerous positions.

His second demonstrated altogether different qualities.

Driving into the penalty area, Cunha unleashed a powerful finish that completed an extraordinary turnaround and transformed Old Trafford's atmosphere.

There was still time for controversy, with the forward receiving a stoppage-time red card after producing the decisive contribution.

United's victory offered Carrick a potentially significant psychological breakthrough. However, their Champions League ambitions will ultimately depend upon developing the defensive consistency absent throughout the opening half.

Tielemans brought composure, Martinez improved distribution and Lacey offered encouraging attacking invention.

For Man United, this extraordinary result could represent an important turning point. Confidence has been fragile, results disappointing and the atmosphere increasingly restless.

Cunha's brilliance provided the decisive intervention, giving Carrick a victory capable of restoring belief within his dressing room.

Roma will reflect upon a commanding position squandered through defensive errors and an inability to contain United's renewed attacking momentum.

Carrick, meanwhile, must ensure that the intensity and conviction displayed after half-time become consistent features of his team's performances.

Old Trafford has witnessed enough false dawns in recent years. This Champions League comeback offers genuine encouragement, provided United can build upon it.

#2694. Dumont family takes controlling ownership of Mavericks after purchasing shares from Miriam Adelson

Sivan and Patrick Dumont are now the controlling owners of the Dallas Mavericks.

The Dumonts purchased Miriam Adelson's shares of the Mavericks last month, according to ESPN's Tim MacMahon, which made them the controlling owners of the team with a 69% ownership share.

Though she has sold her shares to the Dumonts, Adelson is still very much connected to the Mavericks. Patrick Dumont, who has served as the Mavericks' governor since the families purchased the team from Mark Cuban in 2023, is Adelson's son-in-law. Sivan is Adelson's daughter.

"It's really about long-term investment in the city of Dallas," Dumont told ESPN on Tuesday. "The Dumont family is really committed to building what we hope is the best arena in the NBA, a really significant investment in the city that will help create the new 40-year home for the Dallas Mavericks, a great experience for our fans and inspire our team to win championships. That's really what we're focused on. We had the opportunity, and we're really excited about it."

Cuban sold the Mavericks to Adelson at a $3.5 billion valuation in 2023, though he still maintains a 27% share of the team. He's since admitted that he regretted selling the Mavericks to Adelson and Dumont in the first place, especially after the Dumonts and Adelson pushed him out of the team's basketball and business operations side. Cuban's comments came in the wake of the Luka Doncic trade, which drew intense backlash from Mavericks fans and resulted in an overhaul of the team.

Dumont, who is the Las Vegas Sands CEO, can purchase another 20% share of the team from Cuban in the future at the same valuation, too, something he said he plans to do.

"I just have to tell you, I love Mark. He's been a great family friend for a really long time," Dumont said. "He's just a super passionate Mavs fan and he's frustrated. I respect it. We're going to hopefully do him proud. That's my goal — to make all of our Mavs fans super proud about the success of the team and win a championship."

The Mavericks are expected to open a new arena at the Valley View Mall site in north Dallas in the coming years, and hope to have a new business office and practice facility to go with it. Dumont has overseen construction of the Venetian Arena in Macao, which is home to the NBA's preseason games in the country.

The Mavericks have played at the American Airlines Center since 2001, and hope to move into the new arena in time for the 2031-32 campaign.

"I think what we bring to Dallas is going to be world class," Dumont said. "My goal is to make the best arena in the NBA. It starts with the court and expands outwards, and I want to make sure the fans have the best experience possible, because we owe it to them."

The Mavericks currently hold a 4-3 record entering a matchup with the San Antonio Spurs on Wednesday night. They've not been to the playoffs since their trip to the NBA Finals with Doncic in 2024, and went just 26-56 last season.

#2693. Bills release safety Gardner-Johnson day after he completes 1-game NFL suspension for spitting

ORCHARD PARK, N.Y. (AP) — The Buffalo Bills released veteran safety C.J. Gardner-Johnson on Tuesday, a day after he completed his one-game NFL suspension for spitting in the direction of Las Vegas Raiders players.

The team did not provide any further details in announcing the move in a statement, though the league discipline and Gardner-Johnson's inconsistent performance were considered to play contributing factors.

Coach Joe Brady was non-committal regarding Gardner-Johnson's status with the team when the NFL issued its suspension as the Bills entered their bye week off two weeks ago. And he sidestepped a question regarding the player on Monday, a day after Buffalo improved to 6-1 following a 36-10 win over Baltimore.

Brady would only say he had no discussions with Gardner-Johnson after the player returned to attend meetings. The NFL also granted the Bills a one-day exemption to carry an additional player through Tuesday.

The team is off until Thursday, when Buffalo resumes practice to prepare to play at Minnesota (6-1) on Monday night.

The 28-year-old signed a one-year contract with the Bills in March, with Buffalo becoming Gardner-Johnson's sixth stop in five seasons, including two separate stints in Philadelphia. Though he won a Super Bowl with the 2024 Eagles, the eighth-year NFL player arrived in Buffalo with an established reputation of being a noted trash-talker and as someone who has on occasion crossed the line with illegal hits.

GM Brandon Beane acknowledged he consulted with coaches and had a lengthy discussion with Gardner-Johnson regarding his reputation before signing him.

Gardner-Johnson's play was in question even before he was ejected for spitting during a post-whistle confrontation in a 33-30 win at Las Vegas on Oct. 18. He started six games at safety and was part of a secondary that was among the NFL's worst against the pass.

Gardner-Johnson apologized to his teammates and Bills fans for spitting by accepting the consequences and saying he has to be better. He lost in his bid to appeal the suspension days later.

On Sunday, veteran backup Damar Hamlin started in place of Gardner-Johnson in an outing the Bills limited the Ravens to 144 total yards — though Baltimore played much of the final three quarters without starter Lamar Jackson (thumb) and backup Tyler Huntley (toe).

Buffalo's secondary also got additional help from practice squad call-ups Geno Stone and Te'Cory Couch.

#2692. Bo Nix has 15 game-winning drives, most ever for a QB in his first three seasons

The Broncos trailed the Chiefs 24-13 with 10 minutes left on Sunday, but anyone who thought the Broncos were out of it hasn't been watching Bo Nix.

Nix led Denver's offense to two touchdowns and a two-point conversion in the fourth quarter of a 28-24 win, marking Nix's 15th career game-winning drive in the fourth quarter or overtime. No quarterback in NFL history has as many game-winning drives in his first three seasons as Nix.

Dak Prescott, who had 14 game-winning drives in his first three seasons, had the previous record. Nix has surpassed Prescott and isn't even halfway through his third season.

A game-winning drive is defined as an offensive scoring drive in the fourth quarter or overtime that puts a team ahead for the final time. Nix had three of them as a rookie in 2024, an NFL-high seven of them last year, and has an NFL-high five of them already this year.

The all-time leader in game-winning drives is Tom Brady, who had 58 of them. It would take Nix many years to catch Brady, but being more than a quarter of the way there through two and a half seasons is an impressive achievement.

New York Rangers goaltender Igor Shesterkin will miss the remainder of the season with a lower-body injury, the team announced on Saturday.

Shesterkin suffered an apparent leg injury in the Rangers' loss to the Washington Capitals on Friday night as his right leg slid awkwardly into the post while scrambling to get back in position. Shesterkin fell to the ice immediately, and he needed assistance to get down the tunnel.

Prior to that loss, the Rangers were off to a terrific 4-1-0 start, and Shesterkin was a driving force behind that success. In just five appearances, Shesterkin posted 3.90 goals saved above average with a .900 high-danger save percentage, according to Natural Stat Trick.

The 2022 Vezina Trophy winner, Shesterkin has put up sparkling numbers since he entered the NHL in 2019-20. In 330 games, Shesterkin boasts a .917 save percentage, a 2.51 GAA and 22 shutouts. Over the last three full seasons from 2023-26, Shesterkin ranked third in goals saved above average with 45.4. Only Connor Hellebuyck and Andrei Vasilevskiy were better in that category.

Shesterkin was a big reason why the Rangers felt they could bounce back from a disappointing 2025-26 season, and losing the star goaltender puts a huge dent in the team's playoff hopes. It doesn't help that backup goalie Joonas Korpisalo is also hurt.

Dylan Garand replaced Shesterkin on Friday night, and Spencer Martin will be recalled from the AHL after recovering from his own injury. With the Rangers playing well early, it wouldn't be a shock to see them explore better replacement options for Shesterkin.

New York won't be able to replace Shesterkin's impact because he's one of the five best goalies in the world. However, the team should be able to upgrade its current goaltending situation, which is a fairly low bar to clear.

First, there are unsigned veterans still on the open market in Petr Mrazek and James Reimer. Neither one was great last season -- hence their availability at the moment -- Reimer and Mrazek could provide a level of stability in the crease that the Rangers simply don't have right now.

New York could also explore trade possibilities, and Minnesota Wild netminder Filip Gustavsson could be a solution there. Jesper Wallstedt is the future of the crease in Minnesota, making Gustavsson more of a luxury. Would the Wild send Gustavsson to New York in exchange for some draft capital it could use to acquire a center?

The one snag in a potential Gustavsson deal is his contract. Gustavsson is in the first year of a deal that pays him $6.8 million over the next five seasons. That's a big commitment for a player who will become a backup when Shesterkin returns.

Obviously, Connor Hellebuyck has been on the trade market for months now, but that trade wouldn't make sense for the Rangers. Hellebuyck is on an expensive long-term deal, and New York would have $20 million tied up in goalies if they made that move, not to mention the astronomical acquisition cost.

However, if you'll allow me to get creative here, it's no secret that the Florida Panthers have pursed Hellebuyck. What if the Panthers traded Jacob Markstrom -- just acquired in the offseason -- to the Rangers in order to make room for Hellebuyck?

Markstrom does have a 20-team no-trade list, so the question is whether New York would be one of his 11 approved teams. Florida flipping Markstrom so quickly seems like a long shot, but the team has taken plenty of big swings in recent history.

#2688. Match Awards from Bayern Munich’s resilient 2-0 win against Atlético Madrid

Bayern Munich came off Der Klassiker even more injury-riddled than they were before, leaving fans worried for their fate in this much-anticipated Champions League away clash against Atlético Madrid. But Bayern, despite a personnel crisis, put every fear to bed and delivered a dominant performance and, for the first time ever, won a Champions League game against Atlético Madrid at the Metropolitano. Our awards from the game:

Atlético put on a very weak showing tonight and allowed Bayern to control the game for the most part. They positioned themselves well in the first half to make it difficult for Bayern to get into the right angles to shoot, but began to unravel in the second half, which was a flurry of constant Bayern chances. That said, of the team, Pubill was playing out of position on the flank and delivered a decent showing, orchestrating one of their few attacks early on. He wins this award for stepping up, but truly, the Atlético team did themselves no favours.

Stanišić has been in a seemingly endless run of poor form, and today was no different. Stanišić killed far too many Bayern attacks and seemed confused going forward. There were poor instances from him defensively as well, which had to be cleaned up by Jonathan Tah. When will it end? And when will Bayern stop playing him? Yes, the injury situation is far from ideal — but Stanišić has been more harmful than helpful as of late.

There is an argument to be made that Dayot Upamecano is, at the moment, the most important player to this Bayern team. Tonight was another unbelievable showing both defensively and going forward. There were countless times Upamecano drove forward and started attacks on his own, escaping pressure from a well-structured Atlético team and making the right decision every time. When he had the ball, the tempo of the game would instantly shift in Bayern's favour. Defensively, it was practically impossible to get past him. He fought for and won almost every ball, tracking back with great speed and putting in tackles that made fans cheer. His header to make it 3-0 should have stood too, as it would have been the cherry atop his performance, but it was bizarrely disallowed.

You'd think performances like his tonight would be rather rare, but Upamecano has shown this level time and time again. He is absolutely up there as one of Bayern's most important players given the manner in which he influences the entire length of the pitch. He could very well have been MOTM, but was only slightly edged out by tonight's pick.

There isn't much to say here. The midfield wasn't particularly impressive tonight, but Tom Bischof delivered a strong performance, unlocking effective passing ranges and progressing the attack. Joshua Kimmich had a decent showing, particularly when going forward, but was outperformed by Bischof tonight. Bayern missed Aleksandar Pavlović's physical presence at times as players were easily muscled off the ball (Alexander Sørloth's little scuffle with Kimmich comes to mind), but regardless, the midfield did its job for the most part.

Again, none of the forwards were particularly impressive tonight. The running theme in the first half was the forwards' inability to get a shot off, and practically everyone missed a sitter at least once. Michael Olise was clearly off his game tonight, losing the ball countless times on the right flank. He must still be recovering from the injury he picked up over the weekend, because he was far from his best.

Harry Kane missed far too much for a striker of his calibre, and his decision-making was quite off today too. He did deliver a brilliant pass to Konrad Laimer to double the lead, but for much of the game, he wasn't particularly great. You come to expect more from the Ballon d'Or winner.

Alphonso Davies played left-wing tonight following Serge Gnabry's injury, and he put in a solid shift, upping the tempo on the left flank and covering for Stanišić as needed. It was a good performance, but again, nothing special.

Karl managed to capitalize on a costly defensive blunder from Atletico Madrid, giving Bayern the lead despite playing poorly prior. He was not adequately involved in the attack and also fluffed many chances in the first half. He did turn things around for himself in the second half, becoming a lot more focused and clinical. Given the goal and the mentality shown to come back, he wins this award.

What a footballer. He was everywhere tonight, and the most effective presence going forward. He made the right passes, found the right spaces, and was the most clinical player on the pitch. His goal encapsulated his performance perfectly: a fearless finish that was completely on point. He orchestrated much of Bayern's chances through the right flank and almost made fans forget that Olise was having an off day. He did all this while tracking back and fighting for balls with his usual engine-like work rate. An inspiring performance that led Bayern to the win, especially in the second half.

What did you think of the picks? Do you agree? Who would you award? What did you think of the game? Tell us everything in the comments below!

#2685. Will Jonathan Taylor, Brian Thomas Jr. get traded? How will Raiders decide on future with Maxx Crosby? What league sources are saying

With just one week left until the 2026 NFL trade deadline, texts and calls are bouncing from front office to front office.

Multiple landscape-shifting trends have already materialized. The Chicago Bears' trade of two first-round draft picks for defensive tackle Jeffery Simmons is the richest and perhaps highest-ceiling move. The New York Giants' fifth-round pick for now-starting quarterback J.J. McCarthy may net the best value.

Since the season's start, the Houston Texans have traded for receiver Marvin Harrison Jr., the Dallas Cowboys have traded for cornerback Joey Porter Jr., the Seattle Seahawks have traded for left guard Quenton Nelson and the San Francisco 49ers have traded for defensive tackle DeForest Buckner.

Yahoo Sports spoke with NFL general managers, salary-cap executives, personnel evaluators and more to take a pulse of the trade deadline landscape. All were granted anonymity due to the competitive implications of the intel. The summary: Expect more moves during the next week. But also consider the average impact of most moves (we're not looking at you, Bears) more conservatively than initial hype may dictate.

"Usually if you're looking at this time of year, a real need, you're probably not filling it," a high-ranking NFC executive said by phone Tuesday. "You might be solidifying it. I call it, patching a leak. … You might not have planned for the Colts to be in a spiral and now their guard who is going to be a UFA, but he comes available.

"Relax and just see if there's any opportunities."

An executive from a second NFC team explained they're "always willing to make moves … if the price is right." But how often is it?

"Unless you're paying up for this stud, do any of these deals really make sense when prices are kind of flying all over the place?" the executive told Yahoo Sports. "That, to me, is never really where the best deals get made. … But if there's a [deal] that's available that feels too good to be true or the other way around, you get an offer you can't refuse?

"I think obviously you have to come into that with eyes wide open."

It's easy to draw parallels between Jacksonville Jaguars receiver Brian Thomas Jr. and Houston Texans receiver Marvin Harrison Jr. That begs the question: Will any team pay for Thomas the second-round draft pick (slightly discounted with a seventh/sixth-round swap) that the Texans paid the Arizona Cardinals for Harrison?

The Jaguars selected Thomas 23rd overall in the 2024 NFL Draft, 19 picks after the Cardinals selected Harrison the same year. Thomas' career peak thus far was higher, with 87 catches for 1,282 yards and 10 touchdowns as a rookie to Harrison's 62 catches for 885 yards and eight touchdowns the same year. Each player's production and catch percentage have fallen since, and Houston banked on a reunion with Harrison's college quarterback, C.J. Stroud, reviving him. Will a fresh start revive Thomas?

"Sometimes we'll scout a player and we'll say, 'This guy is going to be better for the second team he plays for than the team that originally [drafts him] just because they kind of need a change of scenery, a wake-up call," one AFC personnel evaluator said. " 'Hey, it didn't work out and your career's about to end' — that kind of pressure.

"He definitely would fall in that category, in my opinion."

At 6-foot-2 7/8, per his scouting combine measurement, with a 4.33 40-yard dash, Thomas' size and speed allure talent evaluators. His catch reliability concerns them, Thomas falling from a 65.4% catch rate as a rookie to 52.7% last year and 45.5% this year. Thomas has also registered 19 drops, including 10 last year, per Pro Football Reference.

From the Kansas City Chiefs to the Pittsburgh Steelers, multiple top-of-their-division teams need a receiver. The Washington Commanders pique the interest of some around the league as a Harrison/Stroud-like fit that would reunite teammates and friends from Daniels' LSU Heisman days. Others wonder if Thomas' inconsistency would hurt Daniels' ability to operate a clean offense more than it'd help give the Commanders another target after Terry McLaurin's season-ending patellar tear. One high-ranking executive noted that a timing and precision offense like Coen's is unlikely to best serve Thomas as a target.

A third-round pick seems roughly what the league expects Thomas to cost, an executive from one NFC team comparing his value to that of George Pickens heading from the Steelers to the Dallas Cowboys in May 2025 for a third-round pick (with a sixth/fifth swap), while an executive from another NFC team thought the Jaguars would need to wait until the pressure of deadline day to command a third rather than a fourth. A high-ranking AFC executive noted that the Jaguars had previously shopped Thomas but earlier this season said they were no longer interested in moving him.

If the Jaguars stay put with Thomas, what will explain clinging to a player with 10 catches for 117 yards and two touchdowns in seven games? Targets aren't Thomas' only value, as the Jaguars aim to create space for fellow receivers like Parker Washington and Jakobi Meyers.

"If you trade him and then now … don't have speed, so now the defenses play more compact, it's just harder," a high-ranking NFC executive said. "It's less space. So with that being said, a third may not be enough. It's like, 'Hey, we're actually a good team. Why would we give this guy up for a third?'"

This question has loomed over the trade deadline since, and really even before, the Baltimore Ravens agreed to send the Las Vegas Raiders two first-round picks for Crosby in March. They infamously reneged after Crosby arrived in Baltimore and took a physical that underscored the degeneration in his knee.

The overwhelming belief around the league since: Crosby does not want to be traded. And when the Raiders opened their season 3-0, giving Crosby the main missing piece of his Raiders experience (wins), two high-ranking AFC executives agreed: Trading Crosby no longer made sense. That sentiment continued to capture conversations with executives while the Raiders were 3-1 and 3-2 before shifting slightly as the Raiders fell below (and then climbed back to) .500. So where do things stand with Crosby, who's recorded three sacks, one forced fumble, one fumble recovery and 18 quarterback hits in eight games?

"They've already traded him once," a high-ranking NFC executive said, "so I'm sure that they would listen."

Sources around the league believe that for an offer like the two first-round picks Baltimore presented, or value equivalent to a first- and second-round pick, the Raiders would pick up the phone. But the sense is not that the Raiders are actively trying to offload Crosby, who provides them value now as well as whenever they transition from Kirk Cousins to rookie first overall pick Fernando Mendoza. Executives painted a picture of what they think the Raiders may be considering: On one hand, assistant general manager Brian Stark came from the Denver Broncos, fresh off seeing how Denver's strong defense helped Bo Nix develop as a rookie. Could that sway his belief on what Mendoza needs? On the other hand, first-year head coach Klint Kubiak is the team's offensive play-caller. The more capital to collect elite linemen and skill players to run his zone scheme, the more he'll be able to execute his offensive vision.

"He's probably more valuable to keep, but if you can get two ones for him, you should flip him," an NFC executive said. "I'd probably just hang on to him because you've shown that you're already better than you thought you were… [and] then let's say Mendoza comes on at the end of the year and looks good?

"You're better off having him in 2027 and 2028 because there's a chance you can make a push at that point."

Jonathan Taylor is the most valuable skill position player in the deadline mix. That doesn't guarantee he'll be traded.

League sources stress that equating the Indianapolis Colts' trade of Nelson and Buckner with a trade of Taylor is disingenuous: Nelson and Buckner were each on expiring contracts, likely to leave this spring in free agency. Taylor signed a two-year, $44 million extension with $39 million guaranteed nearly three months ago. He's 27 years old to Nelson and Buckner's 30 and 32, respectively. And he could be a building block for a new regime that already fired general manager Chris Ballard and seems to view head coach Shane Steichen's long-term future with serious questions.

Executives from multiple teams believe Taylor should command something similar to what the 49ers paid for Christian McCaffrey. On Oct. 20, 2022, the 49ers sent the Carolina Panthers 2023 second-, third- and fourth-round picks as well as a 2024 fifth-round pick in exchange for McCaffrey, who has since earned All-Pro honors in both of his healthy seasons.

Two caveats suggest the price could be a little lighter for Taylor than McCaffrey. First, McCaffrey's heavier usage in the passing game offsets concerns about the depreciating value of aging running backs in ways that Taylor's style might not. Secondly, the Niners were bidding against their division-rival Los Angeles Rams for McCaffrey in 2022: That auction drove the price up. Will anyone pay the Colts what it takes? Some league sources point to the Minnesota Vikings as a team that makes sense. Their defense ranks first in points allowed and second in yardage, playing like a true Super Bowl-contending unit. Their offense, meanwhile, is struggling at 27th in points scored and 29th in yards gained. The Seattle Seahawks have raised eyebrows too, though the Seahawks just showed a disinterest in paying big for Kenneth Walker III this spring. Notably, first-year Vikings general manager Nolan Teasley was part of the Seattle group that let Walker walk.

"He's a rare exception of somebody like a running back who makes such a difference that you just ... whatever they want, you just pay it because they have potential to make a run this year if they get a guy like him," an NFC executive said of the Vikings. "If they don't, they're going to stall out. They know that because they know their passing game isn't good enough right now. …

"While you got the bull by the horns, you should try to be aggressive to go, at least make sure you get to the divisional round in the playoffs."

An AFC executive underscored why the Colts should trade Taylor as well as receiver Josh Downs, rather than taking picks for only Buckner and Nelson.

"Teams that do the best job on these trades is really understanding what phase you're in and stacking," the executive said. "All of those picks combined make an intriguing rebuild. One extra third-round pick doesn't really help you."

No one's suggesting that the current iteration of Eagles running back Saquon Barkley nor Titans running back Tony Pollard can elevate a team like Taylor can. Each would be cheaper than Taylor accordingly, but Barkley no longer makes sense for a trade. League sources weren't surprised to hear Barkley say on Sunday night that he's been told he won't be traded. While overwhelming league sentiment is that the Eagles should aim to recoup value, and especially salary cap space from their roster, amid their injury-riddled lost season, Barkley's hamstring and back injuries tank his value likely beyond the point of a helpful return. Before his injuries worsened, executives pegged Barkley's value with his contract as ranging from a second to a fourth-round pick.

Hurting the Eagles' case is that while some positions last well from season to season, the league's view on running-back depreciation tends to limit running-back trades to teams wanting to maximize their acquisition this year. Barkley's limitations hamper that hope.

"That is one position the draft always looks better because age is such a negative thing," an AFC talent evaluator said. "And I'd say running back or skill positions like receiver, usually the need is immediate so they don't compare. If someone acquired Saquon or [Taylor], I think it'll be for this season more than anything."

The Eagles still could shop players. Defensive tackle Moro Ojomo, tight end Dallas Goedert and offensive lineman Tyler Steen are all in the last year of their contracts. Ojomo drew high-value interest before the season, per a league source, but the Eagles declined. With their 2026 season spiraling, would they reconsider sending Ojomo away for something like a second-round pick?

"I think they would probably take the second now," a high-ranking executive from another NFC team said. "But probably going into the year, they'd be like, OK, if we're winning, you're at least planning on trying to win. And then you're like, 'Well, we're not.'"

To round out the running back conversation, Pollard is a cost-effective, healthy and still potentially valuable back who could give a team solid depth. His 595 yards and six touchdowns rushing this season each rank ninth in the league, and Tennessee could seek value for a player likely to walk this spring anyway. A team renting Pollard for the second half of the season might need to pay a fourth or slightly more to award the Titans more than the compensatory pick they'd otherwise get.

League wisdom says the last winless team, the Los Angeles Chargers, should trade players before the deadline to amass the capital needed to rebound from their 0-7 start. But who would this franchise trade? Edge rusher Tuli Tuipulotu is in the final year of his rookie deal, following up his 2025 13-sack season with an interception, two forced fumbles and a fumble recovery in seven games so far. He also leads all edge rushers in run-stop win rate, per ESPN's metric. Executives from multiple teams think he'd draw value akin to a second-round draft pick even with just half a year left on his deal. But trading away young edge rushers is a risky proposition, and the Chargers are "a relatively conservative bunch," as one high-ranking NFC executive said. Executives and evaluators believe it would make little sense, however, for the Chargers not to offload 35-year-old Khalil Mack. He's also up after this season and regardless of the pick back, trading the remainder of Mack's $18 million salary is worth it, they say. Mack could help a team needing pass rush, but at this stage of his career, "I wouldn't count on him as a game-changer," the high-ranking NFC executive said.

Falcons safety Jessie Bates III could be a win-win option for a contending team. The Falcons drafted safety Xavier Watts in the third round last year and safety Billy Bowman in the fourth last year before trading for Sydney Brown this spring. Atlanta's depth at the position, paired with their 3-5 record and quarterback questions, should help the Falcons rationalize trading away an impact defender. In eight games, Bates has 46 tackles, three forced fumbles, one fumble recovery touchdown and one interception. He could immediately elevate a contender that's currently stronger on offense than defense. One NFC executive pointed to the Buffalo Bills as a fit to narrow the gap between their powerhouse offense and shaky defense, while an executive from another NFC team thought the Bills would be more interested in pass-rushing help. (The Bills released safety C.J. Gardner-Johnson on Tuesday, opening another potential case for Bates.) Executives pegged the likely price to rent Bates at a third-round pick, with the possibility to creep to a second.

Executives across the league remain split on whether they'd have traded two first-round picks for Jeffery Simmons, who starred in his Monday night debut with the Chicago Bears. Simmons' six tackles, one sack, two tackles for loss and pass deflection wreaked havoc on the Seahawks in a 34-17 decision. Some executives believe the price was too steep, pegging Simmons' value as closer to a first- and second-round pick or "one and change." The Bears became the first team in the modern draft era to spend two first-round picks on an interior defensive lineman. But one high-ranking NFC executive said they respect the Bears recognizing their window and chasing it. A talent evaluator from another NFC team explained why they're more comfortable trading for a 29-year-old defensive tackle than a speed rusher.  "As a speed rusher, there is going to be a level of depreciation that you're going to expect from this player regardless … " the evaluator said. "These large prototype, explosive, powerful defensive linemen I would say do tend to have a level of normal regression that I think can protect your investment."

#2684. Brewers win the 2026 World Series: Where the Brew Crew ranks among the best recent MLB champions

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

ST. PETERSBURG -- The Milwaukee Brewers are World Series champions. There's so much weight in such a statement on its own, but let's consider for a second all the context behind it.

The 2026 Brewers won 103 games in the regular season and then, more impressively, went a ridiculous 11-2 in the playoffs, never facing elimination, never even trailing in a series. They were one loss away Not only that, but they came so close to being the first team ever to go 8-0 in the League Championship Series and World Series. The 1976 Reds were the only team to sweep both the LCS and World Series, but that only got them to 7-0 because the LCS was five games until 1985. The best playoff record in the era of multiple wild cards was the 2022 Astros at 11-2, and the Brewers have tied that. The 2005 White Sox went 11-1 and so did the 1999 Yankees. We're already up in rarefied air. But there's more.

Think about how hot the Brewers closed. They finished the regular season by winning 15 of their last 18 games. This means they went 26-5 after Sept. 6. Further, look at who they decimated in the playoffs. The Padres were riding a run of 19 wins in 22 games, including a two-game sweep in the Wild Card Series. The Brewers went 3-1 in that NLDS. The Dodgers were the two-time defending champions who swept the Brewers in the NLCS last year. They won 100 games in 2026. The Brewers swept them in four games. The Rays won 98 games in the regular season and were 7-2 thus far in the playoffs. The Brewers took them down in five with their only loss coming in 12 innings.

Remember the Bob Uecker line from "Major League?" There's nothing left but a vapor trail.

That's the Brewers' path to the championship. They just became an absolute killing machine down the stretch, pulverizing everything in their path.

Statistically, they can't touch the 1998 Yankees (114 wins, +309 run differential, 11-2 playoff record including World Series sweep) and certainly can't get to the 1927 Yankees (110-44, +376 run differential, swept World Series). But what about more recently?

Such an exercise is subjective, but let's figure out where these Brewers rank in recent memory. Probably really close to the top, if not all the way up. This wasn't a team loaded with future Hall of Famers, as the Dodgers were last season, for example, but the numbers say these Brewers take a back seat to very few, if any, teams in the past couple of decades.

In fact, let's sort through it. I'll go with the multiple-wild card era, so we're starting in 2012. Let's narrow it down to teams that won at least 100 games and also won the World Series. Yes, the World Series title is a requirement, so we can safely say goodbye to the 2021 Giants and 2022 Dodgers.

We'll compare the teams via regular-season record, run differential, playoff record and how they fared in the World Series. As you'll see, the Brewers will have the most impressive resume here.

An absolute juggernaut in the regular season outside of a wretched stretch before the All-Star break, the Cubs finally broke the faux curse and won it all. They had the regular-season MVP and two Cy Young candidates, in addition to the Cy Young winner from the previous year. On the downside of this argument, they trailed in both the NLCS and World Series (three games to one). Coming back is impressive, but the most dominant teams didn't fall behind.

The first World Series title in franchise history came with a young and (at least it felt like it at the time) fun team. They had the MVP and a former Cy Young winner and also traded for future Hall of Famer Justin Verlander. They needed seven games in both the ALCS and World Series.

The highest win total on the list is right here. They also never faced elimination in the playoffs, though they did trail 1-0 in the ALCS. The MVP of the league was again on the champs and they also had three Cy Young winners (Chris Sale hadn't won his yet, but he was the undisputed ace).

After a 106-win regular season, the Astros steamrolled through the American League side of the bracket, going 7-0. They did lose Games 1 and 3, though, to fall behind 2-1 in the World Series after seeing the Phillies club them for a bunch of home runs in a 7-0 Game 3 win. The Astros righted the ship thereafter, though, and won the next three games, including two nail-biters.

Though the regular seasons are pretty comparable in that chart above, the Brewers were easily the top dog in the postseason. They lost one game between the NLCS and World Series.

We should probably loop in the 2013 Red Sox, the 2015 Royals and the repeat champion 2024-25 Dodgers as well.

If I had to rank them, I think the Mount Rushmore in this era would be:

The 2025 Dodgers were a tough omission, but they didn't even earn a bye due to a relatively low regular-season win total.

I'm willing to hear arguments for the Brewers over that Red Sox team, too. After all, the Red Sox did lose a whole three playoff games, even though they never faced elimination.

The bottom line is that the 2026 Milwaukee Brewers are one of the best, if not the greatest, champions in recent history.

#2682. NBA rumors: Injury-plagued Thunder eyeing player 'they've already had,' and one surging star makes most sense

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Last season, a total of 11 players gave the Oklahoma City Thunder at least 900 minutes of service. Three of those players now play for other teams: Lu Dort, Aaron Wiggins and Isaiah Joe. Two of them, Jalen Williams and Cason Wallace, have already suffered injuries that may end their seasons. Another, Alex Caruso, has a sprained ankle. For Wednesday's game against the Dallas Mavericks, Chet Holmgren is also out with right knee patellar tendinitis and Ajay Mitchell is questionable with a right ankle sprain.

In other words, most of Oklahoma City's core rotation from a year ago, aside from Shai Gilgeous-Alexander, is not available right now. Inevitably, that has sparked quite a bit of speculation. The Thunder are as asset-rich as any team in the NBA. They have the picks to go trade for a difference-maker and a roster spot to add a free agent. The question here is who, and on Wednesday, ESPN's Brian Windhorst stirred the pot with an intentionally cryptic rumor.

"And this is one thing that I've talked to executives about, and I don't mean to be cryptic, but I'm being cryptic," he said on his Hoop Collective podcast. "If you're going to, if they're going to acquire a player, it would not be a surprise if they acquire a player they've already had."

This makes plenty of sense on paper. The Thunder are very particular about their culture. Bringing in someone new is far riskier than reacquiring someone they already know, and given their asset surplus, they can afford to be picky. Given Windhorst's track record of cryptic reporting leading to seismic transactions, let's take a look around the league to see which former Thunder players, if any, make sense as reacquisition targets.

The Thunder traded Dort, Joe and Wiggins last offseason. Given how things have played out, Oklahoma City may regret doing so, and given this rumor cycle, fans will inevitably call for them to try to reacquire one of last season's core pieces. Alas, Dort, Joe and Wiggins are functionally not obtainable to the Thunder. The NBA does not allow teams to reacquire players they have traded until the following season. That means Dort, Joe and Wiggins are off limits for now.

There is a very narrow exception to this rule, but it is not likely to come up. If the player is traded a second time and then gets waived, the original team can re-sign him upon clearing waivers. This happened with Mike Conley and the Minnesota Timberwolves last season. Of course, no team is likely to waive Dort, Joe or Wiggins, so we should assume for the sake of argument that they are off the table.

The Thunder have been so well-run for so long that the NBA is now littered with extremely accomplished Thunder alumni. Of course, these players are, in most cases, either so expensive that they would be impractical for Oklahoma City's purposes or so vital to their existing teams that they likely are not functionally available. So let's roll through those players now:

The players listed above are all currently under contract with teams trying to win today. There are, however, quite a few famous Thunder alumni who are theoretically much more gettable. Four stand out:

A reporter asked general manager Sam Presti on Monday about potentially bringing back retired team legend Russell Westbrook. Presti gave a typical non-answer. Fans would certainly love to see Westbrook in a Thunder uniform again, but the question here is whether he'd be able to accept a small enough role for this to be worthwhile. Westbrook, who announced his retirement in August, is a high-usage player whose value is mostly derived from having the ball in his hands. His issues as a shooter are well-documented, and while he's capable of the sort of intense on-ball defense the Thunder prefer, he's never been consistent as a team defender. All in all, Westbrook is probably just too high-maintenance an addition given what the Thunder could expect out of a 37-year-old.

The point guard Westbrook was once traded for, Chris Paul, makes a bit more sense. He and Gilgeous-Alexander thrived together during the 2019-20 season. However, Paul fell off a cliff during his brief return to the Clippers last season, and he's a notoriously demanding locker-room presence. He's now 41 and has shown no interest in playing in the NBA again after announcing his retirement in February, so we can probably cross him off the list.

Here's a sneaky one: Victor Oladipo. He spent this offseason trying to fight his way back onto an NBA roster. The Sacramento Kings worked him out, but did not sign him. He has not played since the 2022-23 season, but is still only 34. The healthy version of him fit into Oklahoma City's defensive culture, and after several years out of the league, he'd likely be happy with any role the Thunder could offer him.

The only non-guard in this section: Al Horford. The Thunder, again, have plenty of front-court depth. If they did elect to trade one of their bigs for help elsewhere, though, Horford is still useful in a smaller role and the Golden State Warriors simply aren't competitive enough to turn away offers for players in their 40s. The Thunder have several trade exceptions big enough to fit Horford, and his salary is just below the $6.9 million in second-apron space they currently have available.

Any of these three players theoretically could have landed in one of the last two categories. For reasons I'll explain, I wanted to separate them:

George is more expensive than any player we've covered thus far. The only scenario in which this would make sense is one in which the Thunder trade Jalen Williams to Boston (along with a few other contracts, for the sake of legality). That, obviously, is enormously unlikely. It just isn't so crazy that it should be taken off the table altogether. The Celtics already showed a willingness to take a step back this season in the name of the longer view when they traded Jaylen Brown for George in the first place. The Thunder, however, have much more at stake this season given their impending financial cliff. George, with his player option, could actually help on that front by potentially renegotiating a slightly longer deal that suits the Thunder's needs. There would have to be draft picks going to Oklahoma City, and George would have to be willing to take a team-friendly contract that pays him less than Williams is due next season. But if you squint hard enough, you can see something that sort of makes sense here.

The Thunder traded Giddey in part because his shooting made him an iffy off-ball fit next to Gilgeous-Alexander. Well, Giddey has made at least 38% of his catch-and-shoot 3s since coming to Chicago. The Bulls have a new front office that didn't bring Giddey in, and he's struggled to start this season. That doesn't mean they'll give up on him, but it means he could be gettable at the right price. Alas, price is the biggest hurdle here. The Thunder have no obvious way to cobble together the $25 million in tradable salary they'd need to match Giddey's contract without incurring an untenable first-apron hard cap. This would have to be a part of something bigger we can't foresee, so it's unlikely, but if the Thunder do something surprising, there might be a pathway here.

The Thunder could fit him into the trade exception they have leftover from sending out Dort, though they'd have to shed money elsewhere to duck the second apron. Schröder would likely be gettable for second-round picks later in the season (especially if Charlotte rookie Christian Anderson shows he can handle real minutes), and he'd simply be a spare ball-handler on point-of-attack pest defensively. He wouldn't have a big role in Oklahoma City, but the Thunder know him and what he brings to the table. Truthfully, though, the Thunder would probably just prefer to stick with what they have... unless things get worse.

Alright, we've spent the bulk of this story writing about players who wouldn't fit. Let's talk about the players who could. There are two standouts here:

The Thunder ironically chose Dieng one selection ahead of Williams in the 2022 NBA Draft, but Williams outplayed him and Dieng could never find a role in a crowded Thunder rotation. That rotation is less crowded now, especially at forward, and Dieng took advantage of all of the extra playing time he got for the Milwaukee Bucks after the trade deadline last season. Dieng has held a much smaller role for the Bucks this season, so he's theoretically gettable. He can't be traded until Dec. 15 because he just signed a free agent contract, but the Thunder likely don't want to rush into a move anyway.

This is the likeliest big swing on the table for Oklahoma City, if any is even possible. Jerome is in the middle of a breakout season for the Memphis Grizzlies and could be well on his way to an All-Star selection. He's also 29, has serious durability concerns, and is functionally on an expiring contract considering his player option. If the Grizzlies view this as a flash in the pan, or a chance to sell high on someone they don't want to give a big contract to next summer, the Thunder could be their chance. His cap figure is only around $9 million, so he's very obtainable. His shooting makes him an easy fit on any roster, and the Thunder have quite a bit of experience managing the workloads of high-impact players with durability concerns like Alex Caruso.

Jerome is a bit duplicative of Ajay Mitchell, but beggars can't be choosers. If the Thunder have to reorient their roster more around offense to maintain this season's title window, they should do so. Oklahoma City has enough of a draft surplus to trade for even an expensive rental. The question simply comes down to whether or not the Grizzlies view Jerome as a long-term fixture or a pleasant surprise they're willing to cash out. The former is likelier, but we can't rule out the latter.

#2681. INTERVIEW: Ex-Dortmund star Patrick Owomoyela on why Jürgen Klopp is "a good fit" for Germany

MÜNCHEN (Bulinews): Ex-Borussia Dortmund star Patrick Owomoyela is confident Jürgen Klopp is the right man who can restore the German national team to it's former glory.

“He is able to change the important things in a short matter of time, and that’s what makes him a good fit," Owomoyela said at a media round in Munich attended by Bulinews.com.

“I wish he could have the Germany guys every day [to practice] but that’s not the case. As I said, he’s able to create an instant impact and a clear vision of what to do.

“Now more than before, his reputation helps players believe what he is saying. All of that is a good fit for a coach with less time but can make things happen.

“It’s just about finding the right people. He used a lot of players [in his first international period] and that will be the case going forward too," the Hamburg native added.

Having played under Klopp at Dortmund for five seasons between 2008 and 2013, Owomoyela gave some fascinating insights into what the 59-year-old demands from his squad.

“He was a coach who pushed for hard work but have fun while doing it. He always had fun it seemed, Even though he asked a lot of us, he would let us have fun as well.

“He was the loudest in the dressing rooms, so he gave you that kind of freedom. But, you had to back it up on the pitch working hard and doing what he asked.

“He could create pictures. He made it really easy to understands where he wanted you to go and what he wanted you to do. It was like a movie in your head.

“So, that kind of ability to get you motivated to do what you need to do, it’s what puts him above many others. He wanted us to play the most intense football.

"It was hunt, hunt, hunt, always hunt. If you got the ball, run fast at your opponent as hard as possible. If they [the opponent] got the ball, go hunt it [back] again.

"He would play games too, if we ran 120 kilometres [as a team] one week, next week he would say let’s do 124 [kilometres]. We believed in what he was saying.

“Even though we lost games and derbies, he would say it doesn’t matter because he felt we were going in the right direction,” he said, speaking with a undeniable passion.

Perhaps the proof is in the pudding. During his time at a once lowly BVB side, he transformed them into a deadly force which claimed two Bundesliga titles and a DFB-Pokal.

Whether that can be replicated on the international stage is up for debate. However, in Owomoyela's mind, Klopp possesses the necessary traits to bring dreams into reality.

#2680. William Contreras named World Series MVP: Brewers catcher impacted 2026 title in multiple ways

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

For the first time in franchise history, the Milwaukee Brewers are World Series champions, and All-Star catcher William Contreras was named World Series MVP. Contreras went 8 for 21 (.381) and drove in four runs in the five-game series. He struck out once. Contreras also went 10 for 14 in ABS challenges behind the plate and 4 for 9 throwing out basestealers.

"I don't have words to say for how I'm feeling," Contreras said through an interpreter following Game 5. "I'm just appreciative of my teammates, appreciative of (manager Pat) Murphy. I want to thank all of them."

Contreras became the 27th player in history with multiple hits in each of the first three games of the World Series. That includes a three-hit effort in Game 3. In Game 1, Contreras had two hits and threw out two basestealers. He was an all-around force for the Brewers. Contreras produced at the plate and dominated defensively.

"This team's not what it is without this guy," ace reliever Aaron Ashby said after Game 5. "He wants to compete every day. He's our bulldog and we love this dude."

Contreras had plenty of competition for World Series MVP. Ashby threw 5 ⅔ scoreless innings in the series. Jackson Chourio went 11 for 24 (.458) in the series. Rookie shortstop Cooper Pratt went 8 for 19 (.421) and at one point had a hit in four consecutive at-bats spanning Games 4 and 5. All were deserving of World Series MVP honors.

The Brewers acquired Contreras in the three-team Sean Murphy trade with the Atlanta Braves and Oakland Athletics in December 2022. That deal has proven to be a heist for Milwaukee. Contreras has emerged as one of the best catchers in baseball and he's gone to two All-Star Games with the Brewers. Now he's World Series MVP.

Contreras is the first catcher to be named World Series MVP since Salvador Perez with the 2015 Kansas City Royals.

#2678. Bruno Fernandes admits Michael Carrick was right to drop him in fiery interview

Bruno Fernandes denied that Manchester United's remarkable comeback win against Roma saved Michael Carrick from the sack but admitted the manager was right to drop him for criticising his tactics last month.

The United captain scored their first goal with a twice-taken penalty as they came from 2-0 down to beat Roma 3-2 and record their first victory in 10 matches.

But after their previous Champions League game, a 4-1 thrashing by Como, Fernandes had blamed Carrick for United's lack of pressing in a post-match interview – and the United manager responded by leaving him as an unused substitute for their next match, a 3-0 loss to Bournemouth.

Michael Carrick had dropped his skipper Bruno Fernandes (Reuters)

And Fernandes addressed the issue in another fiery post-match interview following the Roma comeback.

Speaking to Amazon Prime Video, he said: "The manager took a decision of making myself be on the bench because I wasn't performing, and that's fair.

"Everyone felt that was a punishment for the words that I had said. And if it was, it was right. The manager is the one that makes the decisions. I have to accept them. I have to go forward with that.

"It doesn't change the belief I have on the manager and on the staff and and every player that is in this club, and it doesn't change my aim to win every f***ing game that I have ahead of me."

Fernandes scored a re-taken penalty and helped inspire United to a comeback win over Roma (Reuters)

Fernandes and Carrick subsequently held talks before the Portuguese was brought back into the team on Saturday against Chelsea.

And as he got increasingly passionate, Fernandes added: "It's been tough. It's been a lot of speculation in the media, a lot of lies around many things that have happened in this club between me and the manager, like that we had cleared the air then after when nothing of that happened."

Carrick has been under pressure as United have only taken seven points in the Premier League this season and had lost their three previous matches in all competitions.

But Fernandes said: "We don't need to save anyone's job. But it was important, he needed that win tonight. The club needed that win, the players needed that win. It's something that we needed as a group of players together with the staff."

#2677. Tyrese Haliburton becomes latest injured NBA star: Pacers guard 'week-to-week' with hamstring strain

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Tyrese Haliburton's return to the Pacers lineup after missing the entire 2025-26 season with an Achilles tear has hit a speed bump, as the All-Star guard deals with a hamstring strain four games into the year.

Pacers coach Rick Carlisle said Wednesday that after meeting with doctors, Haliburton would be considered "week-to-week" with his hamstring strain and is unlikely to play in the next two weeks.

"It's not good news, but it could be worse," Carlisle told reporters (via the Indianapolis Star).

Haliburton, who sat out all of last season after suffering a torn Achilles in Game 7 of the 2025 NBA Finals, has been terrific for the Pacers in his return to the court, averaging 21.8 points, 9.5 assists and 4.5 rebounds per game on 51.6/37.0/86.7 shooting splits over Indiana's first four games. After hitting some clutch shots in the opener, Haliburton was overcome with emotion thinking about his journey back to the basketball court, and now he will have to find that patience once again as he waits for his hamstring to heal enough to play again.

The Pacers will be without Haliburton for a big game on Wednesday night against the 76ers, with games against the Heat, Nets and Hawks up on the schedule over the next week.

Indiana will try to navigate that stretch not only without their star guard, but with Ivica Zubac and TJ McConnell as players also listed as out on Wednesday's injury report, while Andrew Nembhard is questionable with a neck/back injury.

That's a considerable amount of Indiana's guard depth that either can't play or will be playing at less than 100 percent, along with their top center. That shifts Pascal Siakam back into a lead role offensively and forces the Pacers into more small-ball lineups with Obi Toppin at the five.

For a team trying to get back into the conversation in the Eastern Conference after a lost season in 2025-26, seeing injuries pile up early in the year is extremely frustrating and disheartening. The Pacers were a half of basketball away from winning a championship when Haliburton tore his Achilles in Game 7 against the Thunder and have spent more than a year waiting to get him back to try to make the climb again.

While Carlisle noted in a radio interview on Wednesday morning the hope was Haliburton's hamstring wouldn't be a long-term injury, soft tissue injuries always bring some concern. The Pacers will have to balance patience with the desire to not fall too far behind in a suddenly stacked East.

Haliburton's injury continues a frustrating trend in the early NBA season, which has seen a tremendous number of top players listed on injury reports. The list of stars currently on the shelf with injuries is staggering, with the likes of Anthony Edwards, Jalen Williams, Paolo Banchero, Kawhi Leonard, Jaren Jackson Jr., Chet Holmgren and Alperen Sengun all currently listed out for games on Wednesday night. That's not to mention players like Brandon Ingram, Jimmy Butler, Kon Knueppel and Kristaps Porzingis who have yet to make their season debuts.

While it feels like an absurd number of injuries this early in the season, it's much closer to par for the course than the NBA would probably like to admit. Stars being injured has become a constant concern in recent years, but there isn't an obvious solution.

The NBA schedule is often discussed as a reason for the volume of injuries, but this early in the season, it's hard to point to the wear-and-tear of an 82-game grind. Instead, it feels more like a byproduct of a style of play that pushes players to their limits. The speed of the game is tremendous now and players are pushing their bodies to play faster and more explosively, which raises the potential for injuries.

That's an even harder thing to solve than schedule reform -- which the league and players aren't particularly interested in -- because playing with pace and maximizing possessions is proven to be the most effective style in the modern era.
